solution_overview:
A restaurant surveyed diners about dietary restrictions. We are given the probabilities of three individual restrictions: Vegetarian ($V$), Gluten-free ($G$), and Dairy-free ($D$). We are also given the probabilities of all pairwise intersections and the probability of all three restrictions.

We define the following probabilities:
$P(V) = 0.25$
$P(G) = 0.18$
$P(D) = 0.15$
$P(V \cap G) = 0.08$
$P(V \cap D) = 0.06$
$P(G \cap D) = 0.05$
$P(V \cap G \cap D) = 0.02$

We will use the Principle of Inclusion-Exclusion for various combinations of these events.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

To find the probability that a diner has at least one dietary restriction, we use the Principle of Inclusion-Exclusion for three events:

$$P(V \cup G \cup D) = P(V) + P(G) + P(D) - [P(V \cap G) + P(V \cap D) + P(G \cap D)] + P(V \cap G \cap D)$$

$$P(V \cup G \cup D) = 0.25 + 0.18 + 0.15 - (0.08 + 0.06 + 0.05) + 0.02$$

$$P(V \cup G \cup D) = 0.58 - 0.19 + 0.02$$

$$P(V \cup G \cup D) = 0.41$$

Thus, the probability is $41\%$. The claim states the probability is above $45\%$, so the statement is False.

**B.** → False

To find the probability that a diner has exactly one dietary restriction, we sum the probabilities of having only $V$, only $G$, or only $D$. This can be calculated using the following formula:

$$P(\text{exactly one}) = P(V) + P(G) + P(D) - 2 \cdot [P(V \cap G) + P(V \cap D) + P(G \cap D)] + 3 \cdot P(V \cap G \cap D)$$

$$P(\text{exactly one}) = 0.25 + 0.18 + 0.15 - 2 \cdot (0.08 + 0.06 + 0.05) + 3 \cdot 0.02$$

$$P(\text{exactly one}) = 0.58 - 2 \cdot (0.19) + 0.06$$

$$P(\text{exactly one}) = 0.58 - 0.38 + 0.06$$

$$P(\text{exactly one}) = 0.26$$

Thus, the probability is $26\%$. The claim states the probability exceeds $30\%$, so the statement is False.

**C.** → False

To find the probability that a diner has exactly two dietary restrictions, we sum the probabilities of having only ($V$ and $G$), only ($V$ and $D$), or only ($G$ and $D$). This can be calculated using the formula:

$$P(\text{exactly two}) = [P(V \cap G) + P(V \cap D) + P(G \cap D)] - 3 \cdot P(V \cap G \cap D)$$

$$P(\text{exactly two}) = (0.08 + 0.06 + 0.05) - 3 \cdot 0.02$$

$$P(\text{exactly two}) = 0.19 - 0.06$$

$$P(\text{exactly two}) = 0.13$$

Thus, the probability is $13\%$. The claim states the probability is at least $15\%$, so the statement is False.

**D.** → False

To find the probability that the diner has none of the three restrictions, we use the complement rule with the probability of having at least one restriction, calculated in part A:

$$P(\text{none}) = 1 - P(V \cup G \cup D)$$

$$P(\text{none}) = 1 - 0.41$$

$$P(\text{none}) = 0.59$$

Thus, the probability is $59\%$. The claim states the probability is under $55\%$, so the statement is False.

**E.** → True

To find the probability that the diner has at least two dietary restrictions, we sum the probability of having exactly two restrictions and the probability of having all three restrictions:

$$P(\text{at least two}) = P(\text{exactly two}) + P(V \cap G \cap D)$$

From part C, $P(\text{exactly two}) = 0.13$. We are given $P(V \cap G \cap D) = 0.02$.

$$P(\text{at least two}) = 0.13 + 0.02$$

$$P(\text{at least two}) = 0.15$$

Thus, the probability is $15\%$. The claim states the probability is under $16\%$, so the statement is True.
